I believe our revenue fell in the first quarter of 2026 against the last quarter of 2025, and my manager wants me to build a machine learning model that predicts revenue. I am the analyst; the result goes to the head of sales, who decides where to spend the next quarter's marketing money. The table I shared is our order export: one row per order, with its date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer. I do not know why revenue fell, or whether the export is complete for the latest months. [shares sales.csv]

I've read the export. Here's what I found before anything is built.

By month it slid from **36,201.62** in December to **32,186.50** (Jan), **26,344.62** (Feb) and **26,122.16** (Mar). On completeness, your worry looks unfounded: the file runs **2025-01-01 to 2026-03-31**, so March goes to month-end. But **50 of 2,020 orders have no amount**, so every revenue figure here is a floor, not an exact total.

Web fell **44,412.09 to 40,371.17**; store was flat (**16,940.93 to 16,858.60**). By region, Dubai lost the most in cash (**40,730.82 to 33,882.27**), while Ajman fell hardest in share (**11,578.89 to 7,764**) and Ras Al Khaimah likewise (**7,249.16 to 5,177.75**); Sharjah barely moved (**17,037.78 to 16,510.67**).

**What needs care before any model is built.** A model that "predicts revenue" will not answer the question your head of sales is actually asking, where to spend next quarter. Your export has no marketing spend, no traffic, no campaign and no price: a model can only re-describe region, channel and category from the past, so it cannot say what would change if the money moved. Two more traps: `status` (paid/refunded/cancelled) is only known after an order finishes, so it must never be a feature — it leaks the answer; and `amount` is the outcome itself.

The honest machine-learning version of your manager's ask exists, and I'd do it as a second step, not the first: forecast each month from 2025 data, hold Q1 2026 back unseen, and compare — that turns "revenue fell" into "revenue fell this much more than this shop's normal seasonality".

**The plan**
1. Pin down the definition of revenue with you (all orders vs paid only, and how to treat the 50 orders with no amount), and confirm March is fully exported from the shop system, not just to the 31st.
2. Checked by confirming the pieces add back to the total drop.
3. Show it as a dashboard the head of sales can refresh each month, with the losing segments called out.
4. Build the seasonal baseline model: train on 2025 months only, predict the held-out Q1 2026, measure the gap between expected and actual by channel. Checked on that unseen quarter, never on the fitted one.
5. Deliver the recommendation: which channel/region to fund, plus one flag for engineering on the app. Stop when the sales lead can name two spending moves and the app drop is either explained or ruled out. If a step fails — for example the holdout is too thin to beat a naive last-quarter average — I say so plainly and hand the decision back to the attribution instead of quoting a weak model.

Three routes are shown above; my pick is the first, since your head of sales needs to know which segment lost the money and why before any forecast is trusted — and the app-channel drop looks large enough that engineering should see it this week. If you'd rather have the standing view first, the second option gives you a dashboard you can refresh each month (I ran into this turn's query limit before I could draw it, so it would be built on your pick).

Which one do you want me to start?

transcript.text: I am the product manager of a travel booking site. We want to know whether offering free cancellation makes fewer people cancel, so we can decide whether to offer it on every trip. The table I shared is our bookings: when each was booked, the travel date, destination, channel, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Today free cancellation is offered on some trips and not on others; partners and our pricing team choose which, nobody assigned it at random. Tell me what you would do to answer this. [shares bookings.csv]

I would treat this as a **causal decision problem**, not a simple cancellation-rate comparison.

In your bookings, free cancellation was chosen by partners and pricing, so trips with it may already differ systematically: destination, price, lead time, channel, seasonality, and traveler mix. The observed cancellation rate for free-cancellation bookings is therefore not automatically the rate we would see if the same trips had offered free cancellation. The key question is: **among otherwise similar bookings, does offering free cancellation change the probability of cancellation?**

There are three things to watch before trusting an answer:

1. **Selection bias**
   The current data may make free cancellation look better or worse than it truly is because the offer is not randomly assigned.

2. **Outcome definition**
   “Cancelled” may mean any cancellation, or cancellation before some cutoff. Free cancellation could also shift cancellations earlier or make them more likely, not less. We should define the horizon clearly.

3. **Decision scope**
   Fewer cancellations may not be enough for a rollout decision. Free cancellation could affect bookings conversion, revenue, and customer satisfaction too. If the goal is “should we offer it everywhere,” the final decision should eventually include revenue impact, not only cancellation rate.

My approach would be:

- First, estimate the effect using the current bookings: crude comparison, then an adjusted comparison using similar trips.
- Second, test whether the adjusted comparison is credible by checking overlap: are there enough similar bookings with and without free cancellation in the same destinations, price ranges, channels, lead-time bands, and booking months?
- Third, if overlap is weak, do not force a conclusion. Then the better path is a small randomized pilot.

### The plan

1. **Define the treatment and outcome**
   Treatment: `free_cancellation`.
   Outcome: `cancelled`, with a clear timing rule using `booking_date`, `travel_date`, and `lead_time_days`.

2. **Compare the raw cancellation rates**
   This gives the unadjusted difference, useful only as context.

3. **Check balance and overlap**
   Compare the two groups on `destination`, `price`, `channel`, `lead_time_days`, `booking_date` month, and `travel_date` seasonality. If certain segments only ever have free cancellation, or never have it, we cannot estimate the effect well there.

4. **Estimate an adjusted causal effect**
   Match or weight similar bookings with and without free cancellation, or fit a regression/propensity model.

5. **Stress-test the result**
   Check whether the answer changes when including different confounders, when segmented by destination or channel, or when using stricter matching. Also be careful about using `nationality` as an adjustment variable: it may be statistically relevant but could be inappropriate for customer-facing policy decisions without compliance review.

6. **Translate into a rollout recommendation**
   If the effect is credible, estimate the impact of expanding free cancellation and compare it against the likely revenue and customer experience effects.

**Stop when** we either have a stable adjusted estimate with enough comparable bookings, or we discover the data are too non-random to answer confidently.

**If a step fails**, especially if overlap is poor, I would not produce a false-precision answer. I would recommend a randomized pilot instead.

The two options I showed are the practical decision fork: use the current table for a preliminary causal diagnostic, or design a cleaner randomized test. If you need an answer soon, I would start with the current-data check.

transcript.text: I lead retention at a subscription company. I want a model that tells us, for each customer, which discount to offer (none, 10 percent or 25 percent) so that they do not leave. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. We have never given discounts before, so there is no record of any offer or of how customers reacted. The retention team would use the result every month. [shares customers.csv]

Here's what I understood, and one thing you should know before we build anything.

**The problem.** You want a monthly, per-customer discount policy: none, 10%, or 25%, whichever best keeps each customer. The retention team would work that list each month.

**What needs care.** The model you're asking for cannot be built from this table, and it's worth being blunt about why. Your data records what happened to customers who were *never* offered anything. To know which discount keeps a given customer, a model has to see customers given different discounts and observe what each did. There is no such variation anywhere in your file — so any model that outputs "25% for this customer" is inventing that answer, not learning it. Anyone who tells you they can train an uplift model on this data is wrong. What the table *can* support is the other half of the decision: who is likely to leave, and who is worth spending margin on. The discount answer comes after a short randomised pilot, which is also the cheapest way to get that answer permanently.

Two smaller things from reading your 1,200 rows: `churned_next_month` has no snapshot or observation date next to it, so I can't tell which month "next" means — I'll assume it's measured from a monthly snapshot, and you'll want that date exported for a clean time-based split. And `monthly_spend` is blank in 48 rows.

**Where the signal already sits.** Churn is 18.1% in consumer (961 customers) versus 14.6% in business (239), and 22.4% on basic (603) against 14.5% premium (228) and 11.1% plus (369). Plan alone separates your base more than segment does — a useful starting point and a sanity check for anything we model.

The plan below starts the risk model now and designs the pilot that unlocks the discount answer later.

**The plan**
1. *Pin the label.* Confirm what date `churned_next_month` is measured from. Check: the churn rate by tenure and by signup month is stable rather than drifting with how recent the row is.
2. *Prepare the table.* Fill or flag the 48 blank spend rows, keep ticket count as-is. Check: row count still 1,200, no feature that could only be known after churn (my leakage check found none, but it can't see a missing snapshot date).
3. *Build a churn-risk model* with a split by time, not by row, trained on the earlier months and scored on the latest. Check: it beats a simple plan-and-tenure rule on held-out months, and reports top-decile hit rate, not just an AUC.
4. Check: the design reaches a decision (which tier gets which offer) within one read-out window.
5. *Then build the assignment model* — the one you actually asked for — on pilot data, refreshed monthly for the retention team. Check: it beats "give 25% to everyone at high risk" on saved customers per euro of discount.

Stop when steps 3 and 4 are signed off and step 6 is running on real offer data.
If a step fails: if the label has no anchor date, we re-export with one before step 3; if a pilot is impossible, we fall back to a rule-based tier policy that rotates offers by signup cohort so the data comes to us instead.

My pick is the first one: the risk model is the part your data genuinely supports today, and its output is what makes the pilot worth designing rather than guessing. The second is better only if you need something to hand finance this week and can wait on the customer list.

Whichever you choose, I'll flag where the discount answer stays out of reach until offer data exists — I won't dress up a model to pretend otherwise.

I looked at your table before saying anything about it — here's how I read the job, and where I'd be careful.

**The problem as I understand it.** You want a score attached to each booking on the day it is made, so operations can decide how many extra seats to sell on each trip. The score is not the decision; it is an input to it. The table holds 1,500 bookings made between 2025-01-01 and 2026-02-24, 343 of them cancelled, and the rate is steady quarter to quarter (21.6% to 23.8%), which is good news for a model.

**Three things need care before any build.**

1. **Your labels are not all final.** Travel dates run on to 2026-08-16, so 324 of the 1,500 bookings are for trips that have not happened yet. Their observed rate is 25.6%, against 22.1% for the 1,176 bookings already travelled. Either the flag means "cancelled so far" rather than "cancelled in the end", or those rows are genuinely different. I am assuming a label is only settled once the travel date has passed, so those 324 rows come out of training and out of validation and become the live scoring set instead. If I instead let them sit in as "not cancelled", the model learns that far-out bookings rarely cancel — and operations overbooks too little exactly where the risk is.
2. **Nationality should not be a model input.** It predicts cancellations, so it will look useful, but overbooking falls on the passenger who shows up late. Scoring people differently by nationality, in effect refusing boarding by nationality, is the sort of thing that should be decided by lawyers, not by whatever improves AUC. I plan to leave it out of the model and use it afterwards to check whether the score treats groups unequally.
3. **Lead time carries real signal** while free cancellation barely does (22.6% against 23.3%) — so a per-booking probability will be modest, and the trip-level spread is what actually sets the seat count. Price is stored as text in your file and needs parsing before use.

**How it could be solved.** A per-booking model plus a trip-level seat rule: what you asked for, and the right route. A trip-level statistical rule alone (quantile of past cancellations per destination) is cheaper, needs no model, and beats many models — worth keeping as the baseline the model must earn its place against. Or you start from the policy and get operations' two costs first, since a probability is useless to them without those.

4. Train on a time split — earlier settled bookings in, the most recent held out, never shuffled. Checked on AUC, calibration, and lift over the base rate, by destination and channel.
5. Turn scores into seats: expected cancellations per trip as the sum of probabilities, overbook at a chosen quantile once operations gives the empty-seat and bump costs and a service target. Backtest against the flat rule on past trips.
6. Fairness check by nationality and by proxies for it, reported before anyone acts on the score.

Stop when the held-out score beats the trip-level baseline and the backtest saves more than the flat rule at operations' costs, with the fairness check reported. If a step fails: no lift over the baseline, ship the statistical trip rule instead; price unparseable, bucket it as text or drop it; operations won't give the costs, deliver probabilities and expected cancellations per trip and stop short of seat numbers.

The real question is "which 50 calls buy back the most revenue," and your own last sentence is the crux: you don't know whether a call changes anyone's mind. Until you do, any ranking is a ranking of *risk times value*, not of *persuadability*. That's a fine way to start, but it should be labelled as such, not sold as targeting.

**What needs care before we build.**
- *Value-weighting is a policy choice.* Ranking by risk × monthly spend will quietly mean low-spend customers are almost never called, month after month. That may be right for you; it should be decided by you, not produced as a side-effect of a formula.
- *City and segment are risky inputs.* They can stand in for where people live and who they are. A retention list that systematically favours one city is a decision you'd have to defend, so I'd test how much the ranking moves without them.
- *Your table can't time-order anything.* There is no observation or cancellation date — signup runs 2022-01-01 to 2025-10-31 and `churned_next_month` is one snapshot per row. - *The permanent fix for the unknown effect is a small experiment.* Holding back a random handful of your 50 costs a little now and tells you within a quarter whether calls work — which is exactly the number your model is guessing at today.

5. That difference is the call effect, and once you have it we replace step 3 with an uplift model that targets only the persuadable.

transcript.text: I am the operations manager of a home appliance retailer. Our support complaints went up by about 30 percent since March, by my own count from the weekly reports. My director wants an AI model to fix this. We have no dataset: the tickets sit in our helpdesk system as free text with a date and an agent name, and nobody has labelled the reasons. I decide what the support team works on next month. What should we do?

Here's what I think you actually need: not a model that "fixes complaints," but the cause of the rise, so next month's team effort lands on something real — and a straight answer for your director about what an AI model can and cannot do here.

Two things to check before any work starts. First, the 30%: it's your own hand count from weekly reports, so before it explains anything it has to mean the same thing on both sides of March — same definition of "complaint," same channels, and whether a seasonal peak, a delivery backlog, or one defective product sits underneath it. Whatever you inherit from that count, every model after it inherits too. Second, the agent name: a report or model that ranks agents by complaint volume is really staff surveillance, and it mostly measures who gets handed the angry customer rather than who causes the problem. I'd leave agent out as a cause. The free text will also hold customer names, addresses and card or serial numbers, worth stripping before anything leaves the helpdesk.

My approach: get the causes first from the text itself, then decide the work list, and only then consider a model that keeps the categories filled in automatically.

**The plan**
1. Verify the rise. Rebuild your hand count as one query over ticket dates, and compare like periods. Checked by: the monthly counts you can reproduce from the weekly reports, and the definition written down.
2. Export and structure the tickets. One table, date plus text plus any product, channel or order reference, personal details removed. Checked by: row count matching the helpdesk's own total for the period.
3. Build a reason taxonomy from the text, then label a sample by hand with your team. Checked by: two people labelling the same small batch and agreeing on nearly every ticket; if they don't, the category list is wrong, not the team.
4. Report which categories moved. Before-March against after-March, by category, showing where the growth sits. Checked by: the categories adding up to the verified total rise.
5. Decide next month's work list from the top causes, and answer the director with what step 3 proved about labels. Checked by: each chosen action naming the category it should reduce, measurable in the month after.
6. Only then, the model: a text classifier that tags new tickets with these reasons. Checked by: how well it matches your team's labels on tickets it has never seen.

The three options above are the ways in: the cause report is step 1 to 4 and my recommendation; the model is step 6 and worth doing once labels exist; the director brief is today's page if the export can't happen this week. If you can tell me whether the helpdesk export is possible and what fields it carries besides date, text and agent, I can start step 1 straight away.

choices.what: You export the tickets (date, free text, plus product, channel or order reference if the helpdesk holds them). I clean them into one table, build a short reason taxonomy from the text itself, label a sample by hand, then compare a month before March with a month after to show which reason categories carry the rise. You get: A ranked list of what actually grew, and next month's support work list built on it. Trade-off: Days, not hours. Effort: Days.

choices.title: Reason-coding model on every ticket
choices.what: A text classifier that tags each new ticket with a reason automatically, so future weekly reports come pre-counted. You get: Ongoing automatic categorisation instead of your hand count. Trade-off: It can only be built and checked after several hundred tickets carry labels, and it predicts a reason - it does not tell you what to fix. Do this second, not first. Effort: Weeks.

You get: Something defensible to hand up this week, with no export needed. Trade-off: Contains no numbers from your tickets, so it commits you to the cause report afterwards. Effort: Today.

transcript.text:
Step 1 of the plan is verifying the rise — and it needs the export, so here is exactly what to pull while that question is settled.

One row per ticket, for as long a window as the helpdesk keeps: created date (and time), the customer's own words in the first message, and any structured field alongside them — product or category, order number, channel (phone, email, chat, in-store), ticket type or status, resolution. Keep a ticket ID so a strange row can be traced back, and strip customer names, addresses and card or serial numbers before it leaves the building. Replies are useful if they come along easily; skip them if they don't.

Two things to settle in your head as you pull it, because they decide how much of the work that follows is worth. First, how far back the text goes: if it stops at March, we lose the before-and-after comparison and I will tell you plainly what the report can and cannot claim. Second, what your weekly reports actually counted as a complaint — every ticket opened, or only the unhappy ones — so write that down; without it the 30% is a number nobody can reproduce, and any cause we find would sit on top of it.

Can you export the free text of the tickets, and how many months back does your helpdesk keep it — and does it also carry product/category, order number or channel, or only date, text and agent name?
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

I've switched us from a live analysis to the written cause-report brief, because there's no table to query yet and you've told me to get on with it. This is the version you can start today from the helpdesk screen, no IT ticket needed. The numbers DCLab computes come later, when a table lands here. **1. Write the complaint definition down before counting anything.** The 30% is a hand tally, so the first job is making it mean the same thing on both sides of March. Decide in one sentence which of these you counted: every ticket opened, only tickets logged as complaints, or only escalations and refunds. Then lay your weekly report figures out by month for as far back as they go. If the monthly line jumps at the same point your definition changed, the "rise" is partly bookkeeping and we say so. **2. Use this draft reason list.** Six families cover most home appliance support, and they're the ones your team can act on:
- Delivery and lead time: late, no date given, no updates while waiting
- Installation and first use: booking, hookup, does not work as expected out of the box
- Product fault: dead on arrival, breaks within warranty, recurring fault on one model
- Returns, refunds and warranty admin: money slow, claim refused, proof of purchase needed
- Billing and order errors: wrong item, wrong charge, missing part or accessory
- Communication: nobody called back, contradictory answers

Keep one "other, unclear" bucket. If it grows large, the list is wrong, not the customers. **3. Code the text by hand on a small sample.** Take a stretch of recent tickets and a similar stretch from before March, and have two people label each on its own, without discussing. Where they disagree, that's the category wording to fix — not a person to correct. Agreement near the end of the batch is your green light to go wider. This is the step that also settles your director's request honestly: labels come from this exercise, so the taxonomy exists before anyone talks about automation. **4. Compare the shape, not just the total.** The question isn't how many tickets, it's which families grew as a share of the whole. Complaints rising while total tickets stay flat means a shift in causes; both rising means a volume problem, likely delivery or one faulty model. Look at the same months last year if you have them, so a seasonal peak isn't mistaken for a breakdown. **5. Leave agent name out of it, and strip personal details out of the text** before any copy leaves the helpdesk. Volume per agent measures who gets handed the angry customer, and a report ranking them will teach your team to log things in a way that flatters them — which poisons every future count. **6. What to tell your director.** The model isn't the fix; it's what you build after step 3 to keep reasons tagged automatically. Ask for one month of the reason report, then a classifier trained on those labels, tested on tickets it has never seen. Bring back a table with one row per ticket — created date, the customer's own words, product or category if it's there, channel, and your reason code from step 3 — and I'll run the before-and-after split by category and show you exactly where the 30% sits.

transcript.text: I run deliveries for a grocery company in Dubai: 12 vans and about 300 orders a day, each with an address and a promised time window. Fuel and driver hours cost too much. A consultant told me to build a prediction model. I have the order log and the vans' GPS traces, but I have not exported them yet. I am the one who plans the routes every morning. Is a prediction model what I need, and what would you do first?

**Straight answer: a prediction model is not what saves your fuel bill.**

What costs you money is the decision you make every morning — which orders go on which van, in what sequence, and when each van leaves. A model that predicts something (travel time, how late an order will be) gives you a better guess about the plan you already chose. It doesn't choose the plan. So your consultant's advice is a supporting piece, not the answer.

**Two things I'd flag before anything gets built.** Your GPS traces record the routes you actually drove. A model trained on them learns your current habits and hands them back as "predictions" — accurate, and no help with cost. Any improvement has to be judged on distance, hours and lateness together. You also can't prove a change worked without today's numbers, and I don't have them: cost per drop, drops per driver-hour, share delivered inside the window.

**The ways this could go.** Measure your log first — you learn where the money actually leaks (empty running, long stops, or detours forced by windows) and get a before-number, for one export of effort. Or settle the routing method on paper first — no data needed, but nothing proven. Or predict travel times per area from the GPS traces — genuinely useful later, for how tight a window you can promise, but it saves nothing on its own. Or the general order-prediction model as your consultant said — the weakest fit for cost. I'd measure first, because that result decides everything after it.

**The plan**
1. You export the two tables — one row per order with its address and promised window, and the van traces with timestamps. Nothing can be measured before this exists as a table here.
2. Turn the traces into stops and match each stop to its order, so every delivery has a distance-to-reach-it and an arrival time against its window. Check the matched count against your expected ~300 a day.
3. Build the baseline: cost per drop, km per drop, drops per driver-hour, and on-time share, split by area, day and time band. Sanity-check the worst day against your own memory of it.
4. Locate the leak: compare the worst against the best groups and see whether the loss is driving distance, waiting time, or windows forcing detours.
5. Test a change on paper, not on the road: re-plan the worst day's orders under the same windows, and compare distance, hours and late count with what you actually drove.
6. Only then, if a forecast would change the morning decision, build that prediction model — for travel time or order volume by area.
7. Hand it back as a morning routine you can run yourself, since you're the one planning.

Stop when one re-planned day beats your actual day on fuel and driver hours with no extra late deliveries, or after three attempts that don't.
If a step fails: if the traces can't be matched to orders, fall back to the order log plus your fuel receipts and measure cost per drop only.

My pick is the first one, and the second is the honest fallback if your export comes out messy. Whatever you choose, the practical blocker is the same: send the two tables here (order log and traces) so DCLab can work on them. And one thing worth knowing while you export — are all ~300 orders already known when you plan in the morning, or do new ones keep arriving during the day?

findings.text: For this fleet, fuel and driver-hour cost are driven mainly by route miles plus time spent per drop: deadhead to the first customer, backtracking, traffic queueing, parking, building access, and idle waiting near promised windows.
The biggest levers are assigning nearby orders to the same van and sequencing drops so tight windows come first, dense clusters stay together, and a van does not re-enter an area later in the day.

In Dubai, route time should not be treated as simple distance; address quality, gated or tower access, peak traffic, weekend patterns, and Ramadan schedule changes can all alter both window reliability and driver hours.

A prediction model by itself will not reduce cost unless it feeds the morning assignment and sequence decisions; without the order log and GPS traces, the planner has no baseline showing where time and fuel are actually lost.
Ask the planner which parts of the morning plan he can legally or practically change: order-to-van swaps, stop order, zone balance, priority customers, or renegotiating time windows when needed.
If new orders arrive after the plan is made, a one-shot route plan will break; the method must allow adding or reshuffling stops without making him rebuild the whole day by hand before dawn.
